parsed_answer.content:
In Java concurrency, managing asynchronous workloads efficiently often boils down to the mechanics of the java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor. When you submit tasks to a thread pool faster than its core threads can process them, those incoming Runnable or Callable tasks are intercepted and held in a BlockingQueue while waiting for an available worker thread. However, finite queues are bound by memory limits and system sizing constraints. When the queue fills up to its maximum capacity, a tipping point is reached where the executor can no longer enqueue new submissions.

At this critical juncture, the ThreadPoolExecutor invokes its configured Rejection Policy via the RejectedExecutionHandler interface. A rejection policy determines the fate of the rejected task and acts as a backpressure mechanism to prevent OutOfMemoryErrors and thread starvation. If you fail to explicitly define a rejection policy, the executor defaults to the AbortPolicy, which abruptly throws a runtime RejectedExecutionException. Understanding these failure modes and configuring custom policies is essential for building resilient, high-throughput backend services that gracefully handle traffic spikes without cascading failures.

items: Queue capacity interacts heavily with corePoolSize and maximumPoolSize; threads are only spawned up to the maximum limit *after* the blocking queue is completely full (unless using a SynchronousQueue).

The CallerRunsPolicy introduces a subtle performance trade-off: by forcing the calling thread (often an I/O or servlet container thread) to execute the task, it temporarily halts the ingestion of new requests, effectively throttling the upstream producer.
Custom RejectedExecutionHandler implementations can be written to publish metrics to Micrometer or Prometheus, capturing exact dropped task counts for operational observability.

parsed_answer.content: A common production antipattern is using an unbounded queue like LinkedBlockingQueue() with a ThreadPoolExecutor. Because the capacity is effectively Integer.MAX_VALUE, the queue will never fill up, meaning maximumPoolSize is completely ignored, and the rejection policy is never triggered. Under heavy load, this invariably leads to a catastrophic java.lang.OutOfMemoryError on the JVM heap as millions of unexecuted tasks accumulate.

title: What happens when a thread pool queue fills up? What is a rejection policy?
